Chapter Details: The architecture, governance, functionality and uptake of government digital payment systems.  21 variables in 4 sections. Contains latest available data. Data collection by Perplexity from a variety of sources.
Definition: Whether the instant payment system is used or can be used for government disbursements to citizens, including social transfers, welfare payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants, and emergency assistance.
Comments: G2P payments via digital channels have limited but active use in Madagascar. The Human Development Cash Transfer (TMDH/HDCT) program distributes payments via Airtel Money (~60% of beneficiaries) and cash (~40%). The World Bank Madagascar Financial Inclusion Project had a sub-component (1.1.1) for digitizing teachers' salaries and student grants; while this activity faced delays and was eventually cancelled/modified (as of 2022), digital civil servant salary payments are being explored. The e-Ariary pilot (May 2025) lists salary disbursements and social transfers as priority use cases. NGO-operated conditional cash transfers via mobile money are well-documented. Government G2P is partially deployed but not at scale for the core public payroll.
revision_notes: Fetched all four originally cited sources; the World Bank restructuring paper, IFC story and e-Ariary news article support the description of limited-but-active G2P digitisation (TMDH cash transfers via Airtel Money, cancelled teacher-salary digitisation sub-component, e-Ariary pilot). The PMC article could not be accessed (reCAPTCHA block) so is not relied upon. Additional 2024-25 searching found the e-Ariary pilot listing salary and social-transfer disbursement among its priority use cases, an AfricaNenda SIIPS 2025 consumer research report on Madagascar's instant payment landscape, and a PayLogic 2024 press release on a new Treasury payment platform, plus evidence that the postal operator Paositra Malagasy channels some G2P payments digitally. None of this evidence shows government-wide, active-use G2P digitisation (still no digitised core civil-service payroll), so "Limited Use" (2) on the 0=Unknown;1=No;2=Limited Use;3=Yes-Active Use scale is confirmed rather than promoted to Active Use.
revised_comments: Government-to-person payments in Madagascar make active but limited use of digital channels. The Tsinjo Aina/Human Development Cash Transfer programme (TMDH) disburses the majority of benefits via Airtel Money, with the remainder paid in cash, and the postal operator Paositra Malagasy channels some further G2P disbursements digitally. The central bank's e-Ariary digital currency pilot, launched in May 2025 for a ten-month trial involving the Treasury, tax administration and state utility Jirama, lists salary disbursements and social transfers among its priority use cases. The Trésor Public has separately deployed a new digital payment platform (2024) to modernise treasury operations. These initiatives point to active but partial digitisation of G2P flows rather than system-wide adoption for core public-sector payroll.

Definition: Whether digital payment systems and access points (apps, USSD, agents) are designed to accommodate persons with disabilities (visual, hearing, mobility, cognitive impairments), and disability-disaggregated coverage rates if data available.
Comments: No evidence of disability-specific access provisions in digital payment systems. Mobile money access in Madagascar is primarily via USSD and basic phones, which provides some accessibility for visually impaired users. However, no dedicated disability access features, standards, or policies for digital payment systems were identified. UNDP/UN Joint Programme social protection work (2020-2022) developed disability screening tools and disability grants as supplements to cash transfer programs, but these are for social protection delivery, not digital payment system design. The e-Ariary pilot documentation does not mention specific disability access features. Financial inclusion strategies do not specifically address disability access in digital payments.
revision_notes: Fetched both originally cited sources: the UNDP/ILO/WFP/UNFPA joint social-protection programme report (2022) covers disability screening tools and supplementary disability grants for cash-transfer targeting, not payment-channel accessibility design, and the central bank's e-Ariary RFI/RFQ (2021) sets out CBDC technical requirements with no accessibility provisions for persons with disabilities. A further search for disability-specific mobile-money or payment accessibility features in Madagascar (screen readers, voice interfaces, tactile terminals) returned no country-specific evidence; the only relevant material found concerned accessibility gaps for visually impaired mobile-money users elsewhere in Africa (e.g. Ghana, Zimbabwe) and a general academic USSD-accessibility framework, none of which is Madagascar-specific. The "No" score (1) on the 0=Unknown;1=No;2=Partial;3=Yes scale is confirmed.
revised_comments: There is no evidence of disability-specific design features, such as screen-reader compatibility, voice interfaces, or tactile terminals, in Madagascar's digital payment systems, including mobile money platforms and the e-Ariary central bank digital currency pilot. Mobile money is accessed predominantly via USSD on basic handsets, which offers some incidental accessibility relative to app-based interfaces, but this is not a deliberate accessibility accommodation. A 2019-2022 UN joint social protection programme developed disability screening tools and supplementary disability grants, but these concern beneficiary targeting within cash-transfer programmes rather than the design of payment access points. No disability-inclusion policy specific to payment systems has been identified.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: No specific provisions for refugee or migrant access to digital payment systems were found. Mobile money registration in Madagascar requires a national ID card, which would exclude refugees and undocumented migrants. Madagascar's financial inclusion strategy focuses on the domestic unbanked population. A quarter of the adult population lacks formal ID, which is a barrier for Malagasy citizens themselves. UNHCR presence in Madagascar is minimal (Madagascar is not a major refugee destination). International remittance receipt is functional via mobile money (e.g., MVola's MFS Africa partnership), which benefits Malagasy diaspora sending money home, but this does not address migrant access within Madagascar. No refugee-specific mobile money scheme or simplified KYC for refugees was documented.
revision_notes: Fetched both originally cited sources; neither the World Bank blog (2022, noting a quarter of Malagasy adults lack formal ID) nor the GSMA MVola case study (2025, on P2P/remittance API compliance) addresses refugee or migrant access to digital payment accounts. Searched UNHCR's "Displaced and Disconnected" mobile-connectivity/KYC country reports and a 2026 UNHCR global comparative analysis on refugee financial access; neither covers Madagascar specifically (the UNHCR series covers Egypt, Jordan, Iraq, Lebanon, Burundi, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Somalia, South Sudan and Sudan). A 2026 Mixed Migration Centre/UNHCR report confirms Madagascar hosts a growing caseload of asylum seekers, notably Pakistani nationals, and is a transit point on the Western Indian Ocean Route, but it does not document their access to mobile money or bank accounts. No Madagascar-specific evidence of refugee/migrant payment access provisions, positive or negative, was located, so the general inference that national-ID-based KYC requirements would exclude non-nationals stands but remains unconfirmed by a source addressing this population directly in Madagascar. "No" (1) on the 0=Unknown;1=No;2=Partial;3=Yes scale is confirmed as the best-supported score, though the evidence base is thin.
revised_comments: Madagascar has no identified provisions enabling refugees, asylum seekers or undocumented migrants to access digital payment accounts. Mobile money registration requires a national identity card, a requirement that would exclude non-nationals without Malagasy documentation; around a quarter of Malagasy citizens themselves lack formal ID, underlining the scale of this barrier even for the domestic population. Madagascar hosts a growing population of asylum seekers, including a substantial Pakistani caseload documented in 2026 mixed-migration research, and serves as a transit point on the Western Indian Ocean Route, but UNHCR's presence and related financial-inclusion programming in the country remain limited relative to major refugee-hosting states elsewhere in Africa. No refugee-specific mobile money scheme, simplified KYC pathway, or UNHCR-facilitated account arrangement has been identified for Madagascar.
